nameStory: The Turkish Snail gets its name from its origins in Turkey and surrounding regions of southeastern Europe and western Asia. This large land snail was named after the area where it was first scientifically described and remains most common in the wild.
description: The Turkish Snail is a large, air-breathing land snail that carries its home on its back in the form of a substantial spiral shell. These are among the bigger snails you might encounter, with robust shells that can house their soft, slimy bodies completely when they retreat inside. Like other members of the Helix family, they're terrestrial snails that breathe air rather than living in water. They're considered edible and are related to the escargot snails used in cooking.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Notably large for a land snail, with a substantial shell that feels heavy and solid when picked up

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Spiral shell coiled in a classic snail shape, with a wide opening where the snail's body emerges

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Soft, moist body that feels slimy to the touch and leaves a shiny trail of mucus when moving

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Two pairs of retractable tentacles on the head - the longer upper pair has eyes at the tips

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides slowly along surfaces using its muscular foot, often extending its head and tentacles to explore

habitat: Given the extremely limited observations in New England (only one recorded), Turkish Snails are likely found in gardens, parks, or areas near human habitation where they may have been accidentally introduced. They would prefer moist, sheltered areas with plenty of vegetation and calcium-rich soil to help build their shells.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture levels rise, emerging from winter hiding spots to feed on fresh vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid conditions, often hiding during hot, dry periods and emerging after rain when the air is moist.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding to build energy reserves before winter, may be seen more frequently during the cooler, damper days.
seasonality.winter: Become dormant and seal themselves inside their shells, hiding under logs, stones, or in soil until spring returns.

funFact: Turkish Snails can live for several years and have the remarkable ability to completely seal themselves inside their shells during dry or cold periods by creating a temporary 'door' made of dried mucus that hardens like a cork!
confusionNotes: With only one observation in New England, Turkish Snails might be confused with other large introduced snail species or native land snails. Look for the substantial size and robust shell construction - most native New England snails are considerably smaller and more delicate.
contextualKnowledge: The Turkish Snail's presence in New England appears to be extremely rare, likely representing accidental introductions rather than established populations. As with many land snails found outside their native range, they may have arrived through plant trade, travel, or other human activities.
compareHints: Since this is the only Helix species recorded in the New England dataset, compare it to other large land snails in the region by focusing on its substantial size and robust shell construction. Turkish Snails are generally larger and more solidly built than most native New England land snails, which tend to be smaller and have more delicate shells.
